properties.name: budget_report reports `exceeded` on a contribution the same day's own measurement superseded — the perf fix updated the fact and never the CONSTRAINS edge
properties.statement:
FOUND 2026-09-11. `budget_report` on `con:loop-status-warm-latency-ms` returns **total 12,502 ms against a 2,000 ms limit, verdict `exceeded`**, from a CONSTRAINS edge stamped `measured_at: 2026-09-05`.

🛑 THE SAME DAY'S OWN MEASUREMENT SAYS THAT BUDGET HOLDS. `fact:the-three-perf-changes-killed-the-multiplier-and-two-budgets-hold-one-misses-on-my-own-derivation` (valid_from 2026-09-05) records, after the three approved perf changes: *"✅ con:loop-status-warm-latency-ms — warm loop_status 1,912 ms vs 2,000 (**was 12,502**)."* It names 12,502 explicitly as the PRE-FIX figure.

**The fix landed, the fact was written, and the CONSTRAINS edge was never updated.** Both budget edges are in this state: the orientation-pass edge carries `contribution: 31000` while the same fact records warm 6,459 / cold 11,103.

⭐ WHY THIS IS THE EXPENSIVE KIND OF STALENESS. A superseded FACT is at least visible as a dated claim someone can re-read. This number lives on an EDGE, is read by a tool that renders a verdict, and the verdict is the opposite of the truth. Nothing reconciles the two: `budget_report` reads the edge and never looks for a later measurement of the same quantity, and the fact that supersedes it does not touch the edge.

📌 IT ALREADY CAUSED A WRONG REPORT, IN THIS SESSION. A tool sweep on 2026-09-10/11 called `budget_report` on both constraints, read `exceeded`, and reported to Anthony that "both declared performance constraints are breached" — presenting a pre-fix number as current, five days after the fix. That is the same shape the capture-session skill names as its central example, and it arrived through a different door: not an unread fact, but a fact that was written correctly while the structured value it superseded stayed put.

⚠️ WHAT I AM NOT DOING, AND WHY. I am NOT rewriting the contributions. Which figure belongs in the budget is a judgement, not a lookup: the same fact records warm 1,912 ms, after-write 6,354 ms, and says plainly that *"most loop_status calls follow a write, so 6,354 ms is what a session usually waits."* A budget named "warm" could honestly take either. That choice is Anthony's, and asserting one silently would be inventing a measurement nobody made.

🛑 NOT ESTABLISHED: whether any other CONSTRAINS edge carries a superseded contribution — only these two were checked — or whether `budget_report` could reasonably be expected to notice. No root-cause pass was run.
